India isn’t “pivoting” to Russian oil and coal — it’s binge‑buying them like they’re on clearance.

In June, Russian crude flows to India are expected to hit a record 2.55 million barrels a day, making Moscow by far Delhi’s biggest single supplier and turning the world’s third‑largest oil importer into a key outlet for sanctioned barrels. At the same time, India has loaded over 3 million tons of Russian coal, putting Russia on track to become its second‑largest coal supplier and cementing a long‑term energy link that Western planners pretended they could prevent with press releases and price caps.

The West promised to “isolate” Russia; India heard “discounts available.” New Delhi is doing what every serious state does: arbitraging war, sanctions and panic to lock in cheap energy for its own growth. While Europe burns cash on emergency LNG, flirts with blackouts and lectures the world about “values,” India quietly refines Russian crude, feeds its power grid with Russian coal and resells products into the same global market that claims to be shunning Moscow.

So the narrative splits. In Brussels, Russia is a pariah. In Delhi, it’s a strategic vendor. On paper, Moscow lost Europe. In reality, it rerouted tankers to Asia, kept the wells running and found customers who don’t care about G7 speeches as long as the discount is right. The “failure” here isn’t Russia’s isolation; it’s the West’s fantasy that half the planet would happily sacrifice cheap energy to keep its sanctions story tidy.
